title: Masculine and feminine — for things too
goal: Getting to know noun gender, using the articles *an* and *na* with the letter changes that come with them, and forming plurals.
bekal: know that every noun is masculine or feminine, and what follows from that
use *an* correctly: *an fear*, *an bhean*, *an t-arán*, *an tsráid*
form and use plurals with *na* and *na h-*

dialogs.title: Comhrá — Sa seomra ranga
dialogs.intro: Budi's first day in Irish class. Aoife, the teacher, points at things around the room while explaining something that has puzzled him since page one of the textbook.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Fáilte isteach, a Bhudi. Seo é an seomra ranga.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Tá gach ainmfhocal fireann nó baineann. Tá "clár" fireann; tá "fuinneog" baineann.
lines.id: Every noun is masculine or feminine. "Clár" is masculine; "fuinneog" is feminine.
lines.literal: is every noun masculine or feminine. is "board" masculine; is "window" feminine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Agus tá séimhiú ar an bhfocal baineann?

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Go díreach. An bhean, an chathaoir, an mhí — ach an fear, an bord, an múinteoir.
lines.id: Exactly. An bhean, an chathaoir, an mhí — but an fear, an bord, an múinteoir.
lines.literal: straight-ly. the woman, the chair, the month — but the man, the table, the teacher.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Agus focal a thosaíonn le guta?
lines.id: And words that start with a vowel?
lines.literal: and word that starts with vowel?

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: An t-arán, an t-uisce — fireann. Ach an oifig, an aimsir — baineann, gan t.
lines.id: An t-arán, an t-uisce — masculine. But an oifig, an aimsir — feminine, no t.
lines.literal: the bread, the water — masculine. but the office, the weather — feminine, without t.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tá sé sin soiléir go leor. Cad é an focal ar na rudaí seo?

lines.text: Cathaoireacha. Tá cathaoir amháin anseo, agus tá deich gcathaoir sa seomra.
lines.id: Cathaoireacha. There's one chair here, and there are ten chairs in the room.

lines.text: Tá na cathaoireacha nua, ach tá na boird an-sean!

notes: **Noun gender has nothing to do with sex.** *Cailín* ("girl") is **masculine**; *stail* ("stallion") is **feminine**. What's marked is a grammatical habit thousands of years old, not a property of the thing. So don't try to guess it from the meaning — learn each noun together with its article: not *bean* but *an bhean*, not *bord* but *an bord*.

**An bhean, an chathaoir — feminine gets séimhiú; an fear, an bord — masculine doesn't.** This is the first and most visible effect. One exception you need to know right away: *d* and *t* are never lenited after *an*, so *an deoch* and *an tine* stay unchanged even though both are feminine.

**An t-arán, but an oifig.** The second effect shows up on words beginning with a vowel: **masculine** words get *t-* in front (*an t-arán*, *an t-uisce*, *an t-am*), **feminine** words get nothing (*an oifig*, *an aimsir*, *an eaglais*). So a *t-* before a vowel is a free clue that the word is masculine.

**Deich gcathaoir — after a number, the noun stays singular.** Notice Aoife says *cathaoireacha* when talking about the chairs in general, but *deich gcathaoir* when counting them. Unlike English, Irish doesn't make a noun plural after a number. *Deich gcathaoir*, not *deich gcathaoireacha*. The number itself brings urú — that's Unit 5.

blocks.title: Two clues that are right nine times out of ten
items: Words ending in **-óg, -eog, -lann, -acht, -íocht, -is** are almost always **feminine**: *fuinneog*, *bróg*, *bialann*, *leabharlann*, *gluaiseacht*, *eaglais*.

Words ending in **-óir, -eoir, -éir, -aí, -í** that name a person who does something are almost always **masculine**: *múinteoir* (teacher), *dochtúir* (doctor), *siúinéir* (carpenter), *rúnaí* (secretary).

Beyond those two groups, there's no reliable rule. English-language dictionaries mark gender *m* (masculine) or *f* (feminine), as in this book — but Irish-only dictionaries write *f* (*firinscneach*, masculine) and *b* (*baininscneach*, feminine), so watch out: there *f* means masculine. Get used to looking for it.

blocks.text: The official names of the two genders are *firinscneach* (FIH-rinsh-nyakh) and *baininscneach* (BAH-ninsh-nyakh). You'll see them in dictionaries, but in everyday speech people just say *fireann* and *baineann*.

Irish has six ways of forming plurals, and no rule decides which word uses which. The good news: the plural is always listed in the dictionary right after the base word, and the six patterns below cover nearly everything.

blocks.title: What you need to know about plurals for now
items: **The plural article is always *na*,** whatever the gender: *na fir*, *na mná*, *na tithe*. Gender stops mattering once a word is plural.
**Words starting with a vowel get *h-* in the plural:** *na hoifigí*, *na héin* (the birds), *na huaireanta* (the hours).
**After a number, don't use the plural.** *Trí leabhar*, not *trí leabhair*. This actually makes life easier: for most everyday sentences you won't need the plural at all.
**Adjectives follow the plural** by adding *-a* or making the ending slender: *fear mór* → *fir mhóra*, *teach nua* → *tithe nua*. You can leave this until A2.

sections.title: Thirty of the most common nouns

blocks.text: Learn them together with their article. The last column marks the gender: **f** for fireann (masculine), **b** for baineann (feminine).

Watch two tricky rows: *an cailín* is **masculine** even though it means "girl", and *an obair* is **feminine** but starts with a vowel, so there's neither a *t-* nor a séimhiú to see — its gender only shows once an adjective follows it.
